content: Indian legal information guide | Women and girls | Check current official law Page 1 INDIAN LEGAL REFERENCE Stalking, Criminal Intimidation and Harassment A detailed guide to laws, protections, complaint routes and remedies for women and girls in India Prepared as a content-focused public legal information guide Legal position checked against primary legislation sources available for this edition. Relevant statutory extracts and clause-by-clause explanations are included below. How to read this document: It contains detailed explanations of the complete provisions most directly relevant to stalking, threats, sexual harassment, cyber abuse, domestic violence and workplace harassment. Some statutory passages are reproduced as extracts; other provisions are explained fully in plain language to make their operation understandable. This is not a reproduction of every section of every Act. Important: This is general legal information, not individual legal advice. For an actual incident, seek assistance from police, a lawyer, a Protection Officer, the Internal Committee/Local Committee, or child-protection authorities as appropriate

. For an actual incident, seek assistance from police, a lawyer, a Protection Officer, the Internal Committee/Local Committee, or child-protection authorities as appropriate. The official Act and Gazette text prevail if there is any difference. Indian legal information guide | Women and girls | Check current official law Page 2 1. What the law can do, and which route may fit Stalking, harassment and intimidation are not dealt with by one single Indian statute. The same conduct may trigger more than one legal route. Criminal law can punish an offender; procedural law governs reporting and investigation; special statutes provide workplace, domestic-violence or child-protection remedies; constitutional guarantees guide the State's duties and interpretation. For an adult woman: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) is the central criminal statute for conduct within its temporal scope. The Information Technology Act, 2000 may apply to certain online acts. The POSH Act may apply to sexual harassment connected with a workplace. The Domestic Violence Act may provide protection orders and other relief where the conduct occurs in a qualifying domestic relationship

. The Domestic Violence Act may provide protection orders and other relief where the conduct occurs in a qualifying domestic relationship. For a girl below 18: the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO) is central where the conduct is sexual in nature. POCSO is gender-neutral and applies to every child. BNS and IT Act provisions may also apply. The Juvenile Justice Act and child-protection systems may provide care and support. A legal classification depends on the exact conduct, intent, age, relationship, evidence, date and jurisdiction. A chatbot or first responder should say that conduct 'may amount to' an offence where the statutory ingredients appear to fit, rather than declaring guilt. Commencement note: BNS, BNSS and BSA came into force on 1 July 2024, subject to the commencement notification and savings provisions. For acts before that date, the former IPC, CrPC and Indian Evidence Act may remain relevant. Do not apply the new law retrospectively without legal analysis. 2

. For acts before that date, the former IPC, CrPC and Indian Evidence Act may remain relevant. Do not apply the new law retrospectively without legal analysis. 2. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: offences against women The BNS replaced the Indian Penal Code for offences committed after the new criminal laws commenced, subject to transitional provisions. The following are the core provisions for stalking, sexual harassment, privacy invasion, threats and intimidation. Section 74: Assault or criminal force to a woman with intent to outrage her modesty The provision criminalises an assault or use of criminal force against a woman where the offender intends to outrage her modesty, or knows that this is likely to be the result. The prosecution must establish the assault or criminal force and the required intention or knowledge. It is not necessary to describe every offensive act as an offence under this section: the legal elements must be assessed in the facts. Punishment: imprisonment of not less than one year, which may extend to five years, and fine

. Punishment: imprisonment of not less than one year, which may extend to five years, and fine. Practical relevance: unwanted physical force, grabbing, touching or other assaultive conduct may require assessment under this section, along with Section 75 or other provisions. The victim's account, contemporaneous messages, witnesses, CCTV and medical evidence may be relevant. Section 75: Sexual harassment A man commits sexual harassment if he does any of the acts specified in the section:  Unwelcome physical contact and advances involving explicit or implicit sexual overtures.  A demand or request for sexual favours.  Showing pornography against the will of a woman.  Making sexually coloured remarks. The provision has separate punishment categories. For the first three categories above, the punishment may extend to three years of rigorous imprisonment, or fine, or both. For sexually coloured remarks, the punishment may extend to one year of imprisonment of either description, or fine, or both. What this means: The conduct must fit one of the statutory categories. The section is not a catch-all for every rude or offensive statement

. What this means: The conduct must fit one of the statutory categories. The section is not a catch-all for every rude or offensive statement. Other provisions, including Section 79, POSH or workplace service rules, may be relevant depending on the facts. Section 76: Assault or criminal force to a woman with intent to disrobe This section applies where a person assaults or uses criminal force against a woman, or abets such an act, with the intention of disrobing her or compelling her to be naked. Punishment: imprisonment of not less than three years and up to seven years, and fine. Section 77: Voyeurism Voyeurism concerns a person who watches, captures an image of, or disseminates an image of a woman engaged in a private act in circumstances where she would ordinarily expect not to be observed by the offender or by another person at the offender's direction

. Indian legal information guide | Women and girls | Check current official law Page 3 The statutory explanation treats a private act as including circumstances where the woman's genitals, posterior or breasts are exposed or covered only in underwear in a place reasonably expected to provide privacy; use of a lavatory; or a sexual act not ordinarily performed in public. Consent to image capture is not consent to circulation. If a woman agreed to the capture of an image or act but did not agree to its dissemination to third persons, dissemination is expressly treated as an offence under this section. Punishment: first conviction, imprisonment from one to three years and fine; subsequent conviction, imprisonment from three to seven years and fine. Section 78: Stalking The statutory definition is specific. A man commits stalking if he does either of the following: (i) follows a woman and contacts, or attempts to contact, her to foster personal interaction repeatedly despite a clear indication of disinterest by her; or (ii) monitors the use by a woman of the internet, e-mail or any other form of electronic communication. The section contains exceptions

. The section contains exceptions. The conduct will not amount to stalking if the accused proves that it was pursued to prevent or detect crime and he had been entrusted by the State with that responsibility; that it was pursued under a law or to comply with a condition or requirement imposed under law; or that, in the particular circumstances, the conduct was reasonable and justified. Punishment: first conviction, imprisonment up to three years and fine; second or subsequent conviction, imprisonment up to five years and fine. Important legal boundary: Section 78 is worded as an offence by 'any man' against 'a woman'. It includes repeated pursuit/contact after a clear indication of disinterest and monitoring electronic communications. It is not correct to describe every unwanted message, isolated contact, or all forms of gender-neutral stalking as automatically satisfying Section 78. Other offences or civil remedies may apply

. It is not correct to describe every unwanted message, isolated contact, or all forms of gender-neutral stalking as automatically satisfying Section 78. Other offences or civil remedies may apply. Section 79: Word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman This section applies where a person, intending to insult a woman's modesty, utters words, makes a sound or gesture, or exhibits an object intending that the woman hear or see it, or intrudes upon her privacy. Punishment: simple imprisonment up to three years and fine. The required intention and the nature of the conduct must be assessed; not every unpleasant remark necessarily meets the legal test. Section 351: Criminal intimidation A person commits criminal intimidation if they threaten another person, by any means, with injury to that person's body, reputation or property, or to the body or reputation of someone in whom that person is interested, with either of these intentions:  to cause alarm to the person threatened; or  to make that person do something they are not legally bound to do, or omit something they are legally entitled to do, as a way of avoiding execution of the threat

. A threat to injure the reputation of a deceased person in whom the threatened person is interested is also included. Ordinary form punishment: imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both. Aggravated threats: where the threat is to cause death or grievous hurt, destruction of property by fire, commission of an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment, or to impute unchastity to a woman, punishment may extend to seven years, or fine, or both. Anonymous threats: where the intimidation is by anonymous communication, or the person takes precautions to conceal their name or abode, an additional punishment of imprisonment up to two years may apply in addition to the punishment under subsection (1). Examples requiring legal assessment: threats to assault a woman, harm her family, damage her home, expose intimate material, destroy her reputation, or force her to withdraw a complaint may potentially fall within Section 351, depending on the threatened injury and intent. A mere angry statement is not automatically criminal intimidation

. A mere angry statement is not automatically criminal intimidation. Section 352: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace This section applies where a person intentionally insults another in a manner that gives provocation, intending or knowing it to be likely that the provocation will cause that person to break the public peace or commit another offence. Punishment: imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both. It is not a general offence for all offensive language. The intention or knowledge concerning provocation and likely breach of peace is essential. Other BNS provisions that may arise in a harassment case Indian legal information guide | Women and girls | Check current official law Page 4 Depending on the conduct, a lawyer or investigator may also need to consider:  Section 61, criminal conspiracy: where two or more persons agree to commit an illegal act or a legal act by illegal means, subject to the statutory ingredients.  Sections 45–60, abetment: where a person instigates, intentionally aids or otherwise abets an offence.  Section 62, attempt: where conduct goes beyond preparation and amounts to an attempt to commit an offence

.  Section 62, attempt: where conduct goes beyond preparation and amounts to an attempt to commit an offence.  Sections 126–127, wrongful restraint and wrongful confinement: where a woman is unlawfully prevented from proceeding in a direction or confined within limits.  Section 308, extortion: may be relevant where a threat is used to dishonestly induce delivery of property or valuable security. Blackmail for money must be assessed against the exact elements.  Sections 85–86, cruelty by husband or relative: may apply to specified cruelty by a husband or his relative, including conduct meeting the statutory definition. The Domestic Violence Act can provide separate civil relief. 3. Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO) POCSO protects every person below 18 years. It is gender-neutral. A girl does not need to have suffered physical touching for all POCSO offences to be considered. Section 11 specifically includes certain non-contact and electronic conduct when accompanied by sexual intent

. Section 11 specifically includes certain non-contact and electronic conduct when accompanied by sexual intent. Section 11: Sexual harassment of a child A person commits sexual harassment upon a child when, with sexual intent, the person does any of the following:  utters a word, makes a sound or gesture, or exhibits an object or part of the body intending that the child hear or see it;  makes a child exhibit their body or any part of it so that the offender or another person can see it;  shows an object to a child in any form or media for pornographic purposes;  repeatedly or constantly follows, watches or contacts a child directly or through electronic, digital or any other means;  threatens to use in any form of media a real or fabricated depiction, electronically, in film, digitally or by another mode, of any part of the child's body or the child's involvement in a sexual act; or  entices a child for pornographic purposes or gives gratification for that purpose. The Act says that whether sexual intent exists is a question of fact

. The Act says that whether sexual intent exists is a question of fact. The context, communications, conduct, age of the child, pattern of contact, sexualised language, threats and surrounding circumstances may all matter. Section 12: Punishment for sexual harassment A person who commits sexual harassment upon a child under Section 11 is punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and is also liable to fine. Sections 3–10: Sexual assault offences Where there is physical sexual contact, POCSO may apply beyond Section 11. Sections 3–4 address penetrative sexual assault and its punishment. Sections 5–6 address aggravated penetrative sexual assault and punishment. Sections 7–8 address sexual assault involving physical contact without penetration and its punishment. Sections 9–10 address aggravated sexual assault and punishment. The aggravated categories include specified circumstances involving persons in authority, trust, institutions, family or repeated abuse, and other circumstances listed in Section 9. The exact facts and statutory definitions must be checked

. The exact facts and statutory definitions must be checked. Sections 13–15: Use of a child for pornographic purposes and storage Section 13 concerns using a child in any form of media for sexual gratification, including representation of the sexual organs of a child, use of a child in real or simulated sexual acts, or indecent or obscene representation of a child, subject to the statutory wording. Section 14 provides punishment for using a child for pornographic purposes. Section 15 addresses storage or possession of pornographic material involving a child in specified circumstances, including intent to share/transmit or commercial purpose. Do not treat all accidental receipt or possession situations as identical; the exact statutory conditions and amendments must be checked. Sections 19–21: Reporting and failure to report Section 19 requires a person, including a child, who has apprehension that an offence under POCSO is likely to be committed or knowledge that such an offence has been committed, to provide information to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police. The information must be recorded as prescribed

. The information must be recorded as prescribed. The child-friendly safeguards in the section require the police to make appropriate arrangements for the child's care and protection and to report the matter to the Child Welfare Committee and Special Court as Indian legal information guide | Women and girls | Check current official law Page 5 provided by law. Section 20 places reporting obligations on personnel of media, studio and photographic facilities who come across material or objects that appear to depict sexual exploitation or abuse of a child. Section 21 provides penalties for failure to report or record a case as required. The Act distinguishes the child's own position and the failure of an institution/person to comply with reporting duties; the detailed statutory exceptions and provisos should be consulted. Sections 22–27: Child privacy, statement and medical examination Section 22 addresses false complaints or false information made with the specified intent to humiliate, extort or threaten, and provides a child-sensitive protection where a child makes a false complaint

. Section 23 regulates media reporting and prohibits disclosure of a child's identity, including name, address, photograph, family details, school, neighbourhood or other particulars that may reveal identity, except as permitted by the Special Court in the child's interest. Sections 24–26 provide safeguards for recording a child's statement. The statement should be recorded at the child's residence or place of choice, as far as practicable by a woman police officer not below the rank specified in the Act, and in the presence of a parent or a person in whom the child has trust and confidence, subject to the Act. The child should not be detained at a police station at night. The officer should not be in uniform while recording the statement. The Act also provides for recording by a Magistrate and additional protections against aggressive questioning or repeated examination. Section 27 provides for medical examination of a child. Where the victim is a girl, the examination must be conducted by a woman doctor. The parent or a person in whom the child has trust and confidence may be present, subject to the statutory provisions

. Where the victim is a girl, the examination must be conducted by a woman doctor. The parent or a person in whom the child has trust and confidence may be present, subject to the statutory provisions. The examination must be carried out with dignity and in accordance with the child's best interests. Sections 28 and 33–40: Special Court and trial protections Section 28 provides for designation of Special Courts. Sections 33–34 set out the Special Court's procedure and powers, including child-sensitive safeguards. Section 35 sets timelines for recording the child's evidence and endeavouring to complete trial within the statutory period. Section 36 requires that the child not see the accused while testifying, where necessary, while ensuring the accused can hear the evidence and communicate with counsel. Section 37 requires in-camera trials. Section 38 permits assistance of an interpreter or expert where required. Section 39 provides for assistance of experts, including professionals and organisations. Section 40 recognises the child's right to assistance of a legal practitioner. Child-safety rule: Never ask a child or caregiver to forward, upload or circulate sexual images as proof

. Section 40 recognises the child's right to assistance of a legal practitioner. Child-safety rule: Never ask a child or caregiver to forward, upload or circulate sexual images as proof. Do not download or duplicate suspected child sexual abuse material. Preserve non-explicit evidence such as account identifiers, message links and timestamps where safe, and report to police/appropriate child-protection authorities. 4. Information Technology Act, 2000: online abuse and privacy The IT Act applies to specified conduct involving computer resources and electronic communications. It does not create one broad offence called 'cyber harassment'. The relevant section depends on what happened. Section 66C: Identity theft This section punishes fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's electronic signature, password or other unique identification feature. It may be relevant where someone takes over or misuses a woman's account credentials or identity feature. Section 66D: Cheating by personation using a computer resource This section applies when a person cheats by personation using a communication device or computer resource

. Section 66D: Cheating by personation using a computer resource This section applies when a person cheats by personation using a communication device or computer resource. Fake profiles alone do not automatically prove this offence; the cheating and personation elements must be established. Section 66E: Violation of privacy The provision addresses intentionally or knowingly capturing, publishing or transmitting an image of the private area of any person without that person's consent, in circumstances violating that person's privacy. It is gender-neutral. Punishment: imprisonment up to three years, or fine up to two lakh rupees, or both. The statutory explanation defines private area and the relevant privacy circumstances. Sections 67, 67A and 67B: obscene, sexually explicit and child sexual material Section 67 punishes publishing or transmitting in electronic form material that is lascivious, appeals to prurient interest, or has the effect of tending to deprave and corrupt persons likely to read, see or hear it, as described by the section. Section 67A addresses publishing or transmitting material containing a sexually explicit act or conduct in electronic form

. Section 67A addresses publishing or transmitting material containing a sexually explicit act or conduct in electronic form. Section 67B addresses electronic material depicting children in sexually explicit acts or conduct and specified related acts, including creating, collecting, seeking, browsing, downloading, advertising, promoting, exchanging or distributing such material and certain online enticement or abuse of children. Indian legal information guide | Women and girls | Check current official law Page 6 The penalties differ for first and subsequent convictions and must be taken from the current statutory text. The fact that a victim is a child also triggers POCSO and may trigger BNS provisions. A chatbot should not state that all intimate-image incidents fall under the same IT Act section. Sections 72 and 72A: confidentiality and disclosure Section 72 addresses breach of confidentiality and privacy by a person who has secured access to electronic records, books, registers, correspondence, information, documents or other material under powers conferred by the IT Act and then discloses it without consent in the circumstances covered

. Section 72A addresses disclosure of personal information in breach of a lawful contract, with intent to cause or knowledge of likely wrongful loss or wrongful gain. These are not general-purpose offences for every private person who shares a message. Section 66A is not a valid offence Do not rely on Section 66A. The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015). It cannot be used as a valid criminal charge for sending offensive messages. This is an important safeguard against outdated legal information. 5. Workplace harassment: POSH Act, 2013 The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 protects an aggrieved woman from sexual harassment at a workplace and establishes complaint mechanisms. It applies to women of any age in the workplace definition, whether employed or not. A woman employed in a dwelling place or house is also covered by the Act's definition

. It applies to women of any age in the workplace definition, whether employed or not. A woman employed in a dwelling place or house is also covered by the Act's definition. What counts as sexual harassment under Section 2(n) Sexual harassment includes one or more unwelcome acts or behaviour, directly or by implication: physical contact and advances; a demand or request for sexual favours; making sexually coloured remarks; showing pornography; or any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature. Section 3: Prevention of sexual harassment No woman shall be subjected to sexual harassment at any workplace. The Act lists circumstances that may amount to sexual harassment when connected with such conduct: an implied or explicit promise of preferential treatment in employment; an implied or explicit threat of detrimental treatment; an implied or explicit threat about present or future employment status; interference with work or creation of an intimidating, offensive or hostile work environment; or humiliating treatment likely to affect health or safety

. Sections 4–8: Internal Committee and Local Committee An employer must constitute an Internal Committee at each workplace or office/administrative unit as required by the Act. The committee has a senior woman employee as Presiding Officer, employee members, and an external member from an NGO/association committed to the cause of women or a person familiar with sexual harassment issues. At least half the members must be women. The Act specifies tenure and eligibility. The District Officer must constitute a Local Committee for areas where an Internal Committee has not been constituted because the establishment has fewer than ten workers, or where the complaint is against the employer. The Local Committee includes a woman Chairperson, a woman member from the area, two members from NGOs or persons familiar with issues relating to sexual harassment, and an ex officio member as prescribed. The Act sets composition, tenure and district-level jurisdiction

. The Act sets composition, tenure and district-level jurisdiction. Section 9: Making a complaint An aggrieved woman may make a written complaint to the Internal Committee or Local Committee, as applicable, within three months from the date of the incident or, for a series of incidents, within three months from the last incident. If she cannot make the complaint in writing, the committee must provide reasonable assistance. The committee may extend the time by up to a further three months if circumstances prevented timely filing and reasons are recorded. Where the aggrieved woman is unable to make a complaint because of physical or mental incapacity, death or otherwise, a legal heir or other person prescribed by the Rules may make it. Section 10: Conciliation Before beginning an inquiry, the committee may, at the written request of the aggrieved woman, take steps to settle the matter through conciliation. Monetary settlement cannot be the basis of conciliation. If a settlement is reached, it is recorded and forwarded as required. If the settlement terms are breached, the committee may proceed with an inquiry or forward the complaint to police, as the Act provides

. If the settlement terms are breached, the committee may proceed with an inquiry or forward the complaint to police, as the Act provides. Section 11: Inquiry Where conciliation is not requested or no settlement is reached, the committee conducts an inquiry in accordance with the service rules applicable to the respondent or the prescribed procedure. The Act gives the committee powers similar to a civil court for Indian legal information guide | Women and girls | Check current official law Page 7 specified purposes, including summoning persons and requiring documents. The inquiry must follow principles of natural justice. If the complaint is against a domestic worker, the Local Committee follows the special procedure in the Act and may forward the matter to police where a prima facie case is made out. Section 12: Interim relief During the inquiry, on the written request of the aggrieved woman, the committee may recommend transfer of the woman or respondent, grant leave to the woman up to the statutory limit in addition to regular leave, or grant other prescribed relief. The employer must implement the recommendation and report compliance

. The employer must implement the recommendation and report compliance. Section 13: Inquiry report and action After inquiry, the committee provides its report to the employer or District Officer within the statutory period and supplies copies to the parties. If the allegation is not proved, it recommends that no action be taken. If proved, it recommends action under service rules and may recommend deduction from the respondent's salary or wages to pay compensation to the aggrieved woman, considering the statutory factors. The employer/District Officer must act within the prescribed period. Sections 14–18: False complaint, compensation, confidentiality and appeal Section 14 allows action for a complaint made maliciously or with knowledge that it is false, or for false evidence or forged/misleading documents. However, inability to substantiate a complaint or provide adequate proof does not by itself attract action. Malicious intent must be established through the inquiry

. However, inability to substantiate a complaint or provide adequate proof does not by itself attract action. Malicious intent must be established through the inquiry. Section 15 lists factors for determining compensation, including mental trauma, pain, suffering and emotional distress; loss of career opportunity; medical expenses; the respondent's income and financial status; and feasibility of payment in lump sum or instalments. Section 16 prohibits publication or making known the complaint contents, identities and addresses of the aggrieved woman, respondent and witnesses, conciliation/inquiry proceedings, recommendations and action taken, except disclosure of information about justice secured without identifying the persons or details protected by the section. Section 17 provides penalty for breach of confidentiality. Section 18 provides an appeal within the statutory period

. Section 17 provides penalty for breach of confidentiality. Section 18 provides an appeal within the statutory period. Section 19: Employer duties The employer must provide a safe working environment; display information about the penal consequences of sexual harassment and the committee's constitution; organise awareness and training; provide facilities to the committee; assist in securing attendance of the respondent and witnesses; make information available; assist the woman if she chooses to file a criminal complaint; initiate action under service rules; and monitor timely submission of committee reports. Section 26: Employer non-compliance An employer who fails to constitute a committee or contravenes specified provisions may be punished with a fine up to fifty thousand rupees. Subsequent conviction for the same offence may attract enhanced punishment, including twice the earlier punishment and possible cancellation, withdrawal or non-renewal of licence/registration, as provided by the Act. POSH is not a substitute for criminal law. A woman may have a workplace complaint and a separate police complaint if the facts disclose an offence

. POSH is not a substitute for criminal law. A woman may have a workplace complaint and a separate police complaint if the facts disclose an offence. The POSH Act's internal inquiry and a criminal investigation are distinct processes. 6. Domestic violence and harassment: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 The Domestic Violence Act (PWDVA) gives civil protection and relief to an aggrieved woman who is, or has been, in a domestic relationship with the respondent and alleges domestic violence. It is not restricted to physical assault. It can cover sexual, verbal/emotional and economic abuse, and threats. Section 2: Who is protected and what is a domestic relationship An aggrieved person is a woman who is or has been in a domestic relationship with the respondent and alleges domestic violence. A domestic relationship exists where two persons live or have lived together in a shared household and are related by consanguinity, marriage, a relationship in the nature of marriage, adoption, or as family members living together as a joint family. The Act defines a child as a person below 18 and includes adopted, step or foster children

. The Act defines a child as a person below 18 and includes adopted, step or foster children. The definitions of respondent and shared household must be read in full, including the proviso and binding judicial interpretation. Section 3: Full meaning of domestic violence Conduct constitutes domestic violence if an act, omission or conduct of the respondent:  harms, injures or endangers, or tends to harm, injure or endanger, the health, safety, life, limb or well-being, whether mental or physical, of the aggrieved woman, including physical abuse, sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse and economic abuse; Indian legal information guide | Women and girls | Check current official law Page 8  harasses, harms, injures or endangers her to coerce her or another person related to her to meet an unlawful demand for dowry, property or valuable security;  threatens her or a person related to her by conduct described in the preceding categories; or  otherwise causes physical or mental injury or harm. The statutory explanations define physical abuse to include conduct causing bodily pain, harm, danger to life, limb or health, including assault, criminal intimidation and criminal force

. The statutory explanations define physical abuse to include conduct causing bodily pain, harm, danger to life, limb or health, including assault, criminal intimidation and criminal force. Sexual abuse includes sexual conduct that abuses, humiliates, degrades or otherwise violates a woman's dignity. Verbal and emotional abuse includes insults, ridicule, humiliation, name-calling, specified insults concerning childbearing or having a male child, and repeated threats to cause physical pain to a person in whom the woman is interested. Economic abuse includes deprivation of financial resources, household necessities, stridhan, property, rent and maintenance; disposal or alienation of assets; and restriction of access to resources or facilities to which she is entitled. Sections 4–11: Reporting and support duties Any person who has reason to believe domestic violence has been, is being, or is likely to be committed may inform the Protection Officer. A person who gives such information in good faith is protected from civil or criminal liability for doing so

. A person who gives such information in good faith is protected from civil or criminal liability for doing so. A police officer, Protection Officer, service provider or Magistrate who receives a complaint or is present when an incident is reported must inform the aggrieved woman of her right to seek protection, residence, monetary, custody and compensation orders; her right to service providers and Protection Officers; her right to free legal services under the Legal Services Authorities Act; and her right to file a criminal complaint where the facts disclose an offence. The Act provides for shelter homes, medical facilities, appointment of Protection Officers and registration of service providers. Protection Officers assist the Magistrate, help prepare a Domestic Incident Report, ensure service of notices, help access legal aid and medical/shelter support, and perform duties assigned by the Act and Rules. Government must publicise the Act and train relevant officials. Section 12: Application to Magistrate The aggrieved woman, a Protection Officer, or another person on her behalf may apply to the Magistrate for one or more reliefs

. Section 12: Application to Magistrate The aggrieved woman, a Protection Officer, or another person on her behalf may apply to the Magistrate for one or more reliefs. The application may include compensation or damages, without preventing a separate civil claim. The Magistrate should ordinarily fix the first hearing within three days of receiving the application and endeavour to dispose of it within sixty days from the first hearing. Section 17: Right to reside in a shared household Every woman in a domestic relationship has a right to reside in the shared household, whether or not she has title, ownership or beneficial interest in it. She cannot be evicted or excluded from the shared household or any part of it by the respondent except according to procedure established by law. Section 18: Protection orders After giving both sides an opportunity to be heard and being prima facie satisfied that domestic violence has occurred or is likely, the Magistrate may make a protection order in favour of the woman

. The order may prohibit the respondent from committing domestic violence; aiding or abetting it; entering the woman's place of employment or, if she is a child, her school or another place she frequents; attempting any form of communication with her, including personal, oral, written, electronic or telephone contact; alienating or operating specified assets, bank lockers or accounts, including stridhan or jointly held property, without leave of the Magistrate; causing violence to dependants, relatives or persons assisting her; or committing another act specified in the order. Section 19: Residence orders The Magistrate may restrain the respondent from dispossessing or disturbing the woman's possession of the shared household; direct the respondent to remove himself from the household in appropriate circumstances; restrain entry into a portion of the household; restrain alienation or disposal of the shared household; or secure alternate accommodation or rent where appropriate. The Magistrate must consider the circumstances and statutory limits. The Act does not confer ownership title merely by granting a residence right

. The Magistrate must consider the circumstances and statutory limits. The Act does not confer ownership title merely by granting a residence right. Section 20: Monetary relief The Magistrate may order monetary relief to meet expenses and losses suffered as a result of domestic violence. This may include loss of earnings, medical expenses, loss caused by destruction or removal of property, and maintenance for the woman and her children, in addition to or along with maintenance under other laws. Relief should be adequate, fair, reasonable and consistent with the standard of living to which the woman is accustomed. The order may direct payment as a lump sum or monthly payments. Section 21: Custody orders The Magistrate may grant temporary custody of a child to the aggrieved woman or a person applying on her behalf and specify visitation arrangements. If visitation may be harmful to the child, the Magistrate may refuse it. This is an interim protection power Indian legal information guide | Women and girls | Check current official law Page 9 and must be considered alongside applicable family-law proceedings

. This is an interim protection power Indian legal information guide | Women and girls | Check current official law Page 9 and must be considered alongside applicable family-law proceedings. Section 22: Compensation orders The Magistrate may direct the respondent to pay compensation and damages for injuries, including mental torture and emotional distress, caused by acts of domestic violence. Section 23: Interim and ex parte orders The Magistrate may pass interim orders considered just and proper. If satisfied that the application prima facie discloses domestic violence or likelihood of domestic violence, the Magistrate may grant an ex parte order on the basis of the woman's affidavit, including protection, residence, monetary, custody or other relief permitted by the Act. Sections 25–32: Duration, other proceedings and breach Orders may be altered, modified or revoked where circumstances require. Relief under the Act may also be sought in other legal proceedings, subject to the Act. Section 31 makes breach of a protection order or interim protection order by the respondent an offence punishable with imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to twenty thousand rupees, or both

. Section 31 makes breach of a protection order or interim protection order by the respondent an offence punishable with imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to twenty thousand rupees, or both. Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 The JJ Act provides a child-protection and welfare framework. A girl who is abused, exploited, threatened, abandoned or otherwise vulnerable may require intervention as a child in need of care and protection. Constitution of India: relevant guarantees  Article 14: equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. State authorities must apply the law equally and cannot act arbitrarily.  Article 15(1): prohibits the State from discriminating against citizens on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them.  Article 15(3): permits the State to make special provisions for women and children.  Article 16: equality of opportunity in matters of public employment, subject to the Constitution.  Article 19: protects specified freedoms of citizens, subject to constitutionally permitted reasonable restrictions. It does not create a right to stalk, threaten or sexually harass another person.  Article 21: protects life and personal liberty. The Supreme Court has interpreted it to include dignity, privacy and bodily autonomy.  Article 21A: provides free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen, relevant to safe access to education.  Article 23: prohibits trafficking in human beings and forced labour

How to report, preserve evidence and pursue justice If there is immediate danger Move to a safer place if possible and contact emergency services or local police. India's emergency response number is 112

. India's emergency response number is 112. Do not meet or confront a person who has threatened violence merely to obtain evidence. Police complaint and FIR The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) governs criminal procedure for new-law offences. Section 173 deals with information relating to cognizable offences. Information may be given to the officer in charge of a police station, including by electronic communication, subject to the statutory process for signing/verification. The provision recognises reporting irrespective of the area where the offence was committed, commonly described as a zero-FIR route. Ask for the information to be recorded and retain the acknowledgement or copy available to you. If police decline to record information about a cognizable offence, BNSS provides escalation to the Superintendent of Police and recourse to the Magistrate under the statutory procedure. A lawyer or legal services authority can help with the correct application and local process.
